> **das Herz is doubly irregular:** it's the only common **neuter** noun that behaves like an N-declension noun, and unlike every masculine N-noun, its accusative stays bare (das Herz, not [WRONG]) — only dative and genitive take the ending, and the genitive adds an extra -s (Herzens, not [WRONG]).

> **Note on der Name:** like das Herz, der Name has an irregular genitive with an extra -s: **des Namens** (not [WRONG]). Acc/Dat are regular: den Namen, dem Namen.
> **Note on der Nachbar:** like der Herr, der Nachbar takes only **-n** (not the "regular" -en) in every oblique case, singular and plural: den/dem/des **Nachbarn**, die **Nachbarn** (not [WRONG]).

> **A small "-n only" exception class:** der Herr and der Nachbar don't fit either pattern above, and both take just **-n** instead of the expected **-en** in the oblique cases (den Herrn/Nachbarn, not [WRONG] in the singular). > **Key idea:** the sentence frame is the same as with modals (Lesson 2) — one conjugated verb in position 2, everything else before the final infinitive. The only addition is **zu**, which belongs directly to the infinitive and never separates from it: [WRONG] is wrong, **aufzustehen** is right (§3.7).

> **Notes on the list:** beginnen and vergessen take **zu + Infinitiv** (German differs from English here — you cannot say [WRONG]). **brauchen** + zu is special: in standard German it appears almost only in **negative or restrictive** contexts — *Du brauchst **nicht** zu kommen* (you don't need to come) or *Ich brauche **nur** zu fragen* (I only need to ask). In affirmative sentences German prefers **müssen** (Lesson 2). The full brauchen + zu system returns in Lesson 12.

When the infinitive is a **separable verb** (Lesson 5), **zu is inserted between the prefix and the verb stem**: aufstehen → **aufzustehen**, never [WRONG]. The zu belongs to the stem; the prefix stays glued in front of it.

An N-noun is a **masculine** noun that takes the ending **-(e)n in every case except the nominative singular**. In the plural the noun itself carries the ending -en, and the article does the work of showing the case. There are no umlaut plurals in the N-Deklination: *der Junge → die Jungen*, not [WRONG].

> **Note (critical):** every non-nominative case adds **-en** (or just **-n** if the noun already ends in -e). There is no genitive -s anywhere in the regular N-Deklination: *des Student**en***, never [WRONG] and never [WRONG]. And the plural of an N-noun always ends in -en or -n.

> **Note (critical):** *brauchen + zu* is only negative or restricted. The affirmative sentence [WRONG] does not exist in standard German — the positive obligation is always **müssen** (*Ich muss gehen*). Keep *brauchen + zu* exclusively in negated, *nur*-restricted, *kaum*, or *erst*-contexts.
